titre: Why avoid the *long spot* after a tight turn?
titreSimple: Why avoid the long spot after a tight turn?
chapo: A tight option can save precious seconds. But asking your horse for a long spot straight away can turn that advantage into a problem.
s1_titre: Before jumping, the horse had to *sit.*
s1_lead: A very tight turn isn’t just a change of direction. It’s a real effort of balance.
s1_p1: To negotiate that curve, your horse has to **shorten his stride, bend his joints more and engage his hindquarters**. He adjusts his bend and organises his body to stay on the line.
s1_p2: We often say he has to “sit”. The tighter the option, the greater that effort of control can be. He has to keep his activity while reducing his scope.
s1_p3: And coming out of the turn, he doesn’t instantly get back the same mechanics he’d have after several strides of canter on a straight line.
s1_photo_alt: Horse and rider cantering through a turn in show jumping
s1_legende: The horse has shortened his stride to turn. He needs to be able to reorganise his canter before the fence.
s1_citation: “His body has just done exactly the opposite of what we ask of him on a long spot.”
zoom_p: In the turn, the horse gathers his energy and controls his line. To cover a long take-off distance, he would then need to **open up his stride a great deal and produce the right amount of push.** It’s this immediate transition that can become tricky.
zoom_note: The drawing illustrates the difference between shortening and lengthening the stride, not an anatomical measurement.
s2_titre: Asking him to stretch out… *right now.*
s2_lead: You’ve barely come out of the turn and you see a long distance. You push to go and get it. Yet your horse isn’t necessarily ready.
s2_p1: He’s just made an effort to collect himself. You’re now asking him to **switch abruptly from a short stride to a big one**, with a take-off spot far from the fence.
s2_p2: He still has to find his line again, his straightness and a canter organised enough to prepare his push. If you demand that change too quickly, he may open up, flatten or lose the quality of his jump.
s2_p3: **It isn’t a question of courage:** it’s a question of mechanics, balance and preparation.
s2_photo_alt: Horse making an effort on the approach to a fence
s2_legende: After a strong demand for collection, a sudden acceleration can disrupt the organisation of the take-off.
s2_r1: The horse opens up and shifts his weight forward.
s2_r2: He lengthens his stride at the expense of his bounce.
s2_r3: The push isn’t enough to cover the take-off.
s2_r4: A rail, a stride squeezed in at the last second or a refusal become possible.
s2_encadre: A bad long spot isn’t necessarily one that leaves from far away. It’s the one you force on your horse when he doesn’t have the means to jump it properly.
s3_titre: One option. *Two ways* to ride the fence.
s3_lead: The same tight turn can lead to two very different approaches. The goal isn’t to save a stride at all costs, but to still have a jump available as you come out of it.
s3_a_label: The long spot asked for too early
s3_a_p: The horse has just shortened a lot. The rider urges him to open up immediately to look for a distant take-off spot. The canter can fall apart and the jump become flatter.
s3_a_res: Avoid: **a distance forced at the expense of balance.**
s3_b_p: One more stride can let him straighten up, keep his impulsion and meet the fence with a suitable take-off rather than a forced one.
s3_b_res: Aim for: **an organised canter and a distance that’s there for you.**
s3_note: Illustrative diagrams: the same tight turn on one rein in both cases. The actual number of strides depends on the line, the horse’s stride length, the fence and his level.
svg1_aria: Top view: a single tight curve to the right, followed by a short straight line to the fence. No counter-curve.
svg2_aria: Forced long spot: a single tight turn to the right, then a sudden demand to stretch out towards the vertical.
svg3_aria: Extra stride: active canter, a single tight turn to the right and a short straight line to the vertical.
s4_p1: After a very tight option, it’s often better to keep an active, balanced canter and let a suitable take-off distance come to you, even if it takes an extra stride.
s4_p2: That stride lets the horse finish his turn, straighten up, stay engaged and prepare his push.
s4_p3: A good-quality jump usually gives a more organised landing, and can let you get away faster to the next fence. **In a jump-off, the quality of the landing counts on the clock too.**
s4_citation: The best round isn’t always the one where you leave out the most strides.
s4_photo_alt: Horse clearing a vertical at a competition
s4_legende: Good preparation makes for a clear jump and a landing that lets you carry on.
attention: shortening the stride doesn’t mean slowing down or killing the canter. The horse must stay active, in front of the leg and available, without rushing.
s5_p1: When a long distance shows up, the reflex is sometimes to go looking for it: bringing your shoulders forward, driving with your seat or speeding up at the last moment.
s5_p2: But that rushing can put even more weight forward and get in the horse’s way just when he’s trying to reorganise himself after the turn.
s5_p3: Keep your position, go with your horse’s balance and maintain steady activity. **The distance should stay the result of the canter and the line, not of a moment of panic.**
s6_titre: And what if the long spot comes up *naturally?*
s6_p1: A long spot isn’t bad in itself. An experienced, powerful and well-balanced horse can take off further away after a turn, if his canter, his line and his preparation allow it.
s6_p2: You need to tell the difference between **going with a long spot that comes up** and **forcing a long spot the horse isn’t ready to jump**.
s6_p3: The right choice takes into account this particular horse, at this precise moment: his strength, his responsiveness, his balance and the fence ahead.
e1_p: Does your exit from the turn let the horse straighten up and arrive straight?
e2_p: Activity and bounce, with no sudden acceleration and no loss of impulsion.
e3_p: Go with the distance that’s there instead of demanding a long spot at all costs.
coach_citation: You’ve just asked your horse to sit down hard to turn. Don’t ask him, a split second later, to stretch out suddenly to go and get a long spot. Give him time to find his mechanics again and produce a real jump.
s7_titre: On the course walk, ask yourself *the right question.*
s7_p1: Don’t just think about the option that shortens the course the most. Ask yourself what balance your horse will come out of the turn in, how many strides will let him get ready and what take-off spot you can reasonably offer him.
s7_p2: **A good jump-off isn’t the one where you ask your horse for the most effort. It’s the one where you let him be fast without putting him in difficulty for nothing.**
r1: A tight turn often calls for a big effort of collection.
r2: The horse can’t always stretch out immediately without losing his balance.
r3: An extra stride can lead to a better jump.
r4: Keep the activity without pushing abruptly.
r5: Go with a natural long spot; don’t force one.
r6: A good-quality landing helps you carry on more efficiently.
